title: Choose REST vs gRPC for internal service communication
description: Select the right inter-service communication protocol for internal microservices handling high-throughput, low-latency requests with strict contracts.

data.text: Your team operates twenty internal microservices in a Kubernetes cluster. Some services exchange thousands of requests per second. Current REST/JSON communication is causing latency spikes under load, and serialization is consuming noticeable CPU. You need to decide whether to optimize REST or migrate to gRPC.

terms.definition: A high-performance RPC framework using HTTP/2 and Protocol Buffers.
Google's language-neutral, platform-neutral extensible mechanism for serializing structured data.
A major revision of HTTP supporting multiplexed streams, server push, and header compression.
Whether you generate the schema from code or the code from a shared schema.

data.title: Common trap
data.text: gRPC is not automatically faster. Without connection pooling, keep-alive tuning, and proper stream handling, you can end up with higher latency than a well-cached REST call.

data.title: REST/JSON versus gRPC for internal traffic

cards.title: REST over HTTP/1.1
cards.description: Widely understood, text-based, with mature ecosystem tooling.
pros: Human-readable for debugging with curl or browser
Works everywhere without client library installation
Simple to test with standard HTTP clients
API gateways and observability tools are REST-native
cons: JSON parsing is CPU-intensive at high QPS
No built-in streaming or bidirectional communication
No formal contract; schema drift is silent
Headers are verbose, increasing payload size

cards.title: gRPC over HTTP/2
cards.description: Binary, contract-first, with streaming and bi-directional support.
pros: Protobuf serialization is 5-10x faster than JSON
Streaming enables server push and real-time data flows
Strict contracts via .proto files prevent schema drift
Multiplexing on a single TCP connection reduces connection overhead
cons: Less transparent debugging; binary payloads need tools
Load balancers and API gateways need HTTP/2 awareness

data.title: gRPC: Protobuf contract for an order service
data.content: Contract-first definition shared across all services in the repo.

data.title: REST: Equivalent OpenAPI fragment
data.content: No code generation contract; clients depend on documentation or SDKs.
data.code:
openapi: 3.0.0
paths:
  /orders/{orderId}:
    get:
      parameters:
        - name: orderId
          in: path
          required: true
          schema:
            type: string
      responses:
        '200':
          description: Order details
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/Order'
components:
  schemas:
    Order:
      type: object
      properties:
        id:
          type: string
        customer_id:
          type: string
        items:
          type: array
        total:
          type: number

items.text: Is internal traffic above 5,000 RPS between services?
Do you need streaming or bidirectional communication?
Is your observability stack compatible with HTTP/2?
Can you enforce schema generation as part of CI/CD?
Are all client languages supported by Protobuf code generation?

data.caption: Serialization overhead increases with payload size
data.definition:
graph LR
    A[Payload] -->|JSON| B[Parse: ~1.5 MB/s per core]
    A -->|Protobuf| C[Parse: ~10 MB/s per core]
    B --> D[Higher CPU]
    C --> E[Lower CPU]
    D --> F[More latency under load]
    E --> G[More throughput per instance]

data.title: Recommended approach: gRPC for service mesh, REST for edge
data.content: Migrate high-throughput internal services to gRPC first: order processing, inventory, and pricing. These have stable contracts and benefit most from serialization speed. Keep REST at the edge for mobile and web clients.

data.title: Migration tip
data.text: Use a sidecar or API gateway to translate REST to gRPC so you can migrate services independently. This avoids a big-bang rewrite.

data.title: Key takeaway
points: Use gRPC when latency, throughput, and contract stability matter.
Use REST at the edge where human readability and broad client support matter.
Protocol choice is secondary to observability, error handling, and retry policy.
data.takeaway: gRPC is an optimization, not a destination. Optimize the hot path first.
